title: Data from: A practical and safer model of nitrogen mustard injury in cornea
abstract: Sulfur mustard (SM) is an alkylating agent used in warfare and terrorism that inflicts devastating ocular injuries. Although the clinical symptoms are well described, the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood, hindering the development of effective treatments. One major roadblock is the lack of a suitable model due to the extremely hazardous nature of SM, which requires strict safety measures. As a safer and practical alternative, we report a novel model that uses mechlorethamine (nitrogen mustard) gel, an FDA-approved topical chemotherapeutic administered by patients at home. Here, we demonstrate its suitability to induce mustard corneal injury in any laboratory. Ex vivo porcine corneas were injured with mechlorethamine gel. Hematoxylin-eosin staining and immunohistochemistry were performed to evaluate the histopathology of SM-like corneal injuries: epithelium thickness and stromal separation, keratocyte and inflammatory cell counts, and expression of inflammation and fibrosis markers. This model showed the characteristic histopathology and expression of cyclooxygenase-2 (inflammation) and fibronectin-1 (fibrosis), which were consistent with other well-established SM-like corneal injury models. Given its ease of implementation and safety, this mechlorethamine model could be used to study the full course of mustard corneal injuries. This model would greatly facilitate mustard injury research, shedding light on new knowledge that would increase our understanding of mustard ocular injuries while investigating novel therapeutics. This model will allow safe evaluation of SM-like corneal injuries within 24 hours, facilitating the identification of early/new molecules that might help to develop novel treatments that could be readily translated into the clinic.

methods:
The purpose of this manuscript was to evaluate whether mechlorethamine gel could be used as an alternative to sulfur mustard injury in the cornea. Therefore, ex vivo porcine corneas were wounded with mechlorethamine gel, and epithelium thickness, epithelium-stroma separation, keratocyte and inflammatory cell counts, and COX-2 and FN1 expression were assessed. 

The data were obtained from microsections of paraffin-embedded corneas, either stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) or by immunohistochemistry (IHC). 

The sections stained with H&E were imaged with a light microscope with 4x, 10x, and 20x objectives. Then, the 4x images were put together to obtain a low-magnification view of the cornea. In ImageJ, the scale was calibrated, and using the tool, the epithelium thickness and epithelial-stroma separation were calculated in the 4x and 10x images. 20x images were used to count how many keratocytes (flat cells) and how many inflammatory cells (round cells) were present in the stroma in an area of 1mm2. 

These data were averaged, standard deviation calculated, and a Student's t-test was performed to determine if any data were significant. 

The sections stained with IHC were imaged with a light microscope at 4x, 10x, and 20x objectives. The positive signal (any brown staining on the slide) was quantified with software as the percentage of positive area per total tissue area or as the number of positive objects (including cells and extracellular matrix components) per mm2 of epithelial and stromal area, respectively, for COX-2 and FN1. These data were averaged, SD calculated, and plotted.
